analysis.one_liner: Expands health coverage through Medicaid, subsidies for private insurance, and sweeping new insurance rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 60-39 and the House approved the Senate version 219-212, with every Republican in both chambers opposed, and President Obama signed it into law on March 23, 2010 as Public Law 111-148.
analysis.plain_summary: This law extends Medicaid to people with incomes up to 133% of the poverty line, gives refundable tax credits to help households earning up to four times the poverty line buy private coverage, and creates state marketplaces to sell it. It bans insurers from denying coverage or charging more for preexisting conditions, bans annual and lifetime dollar caps, lets young adults stay on a parent's plan until 26, and requires plans to cover preventive care with no out-of-pocket cost. To pay for it, it requires most people to carry insurance, fines large employers who do not offer coverage, and collects fees from health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and medical device makers, plus a small Medicare tax increase on high earners.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and low-income people gain the most: Medicaid expansion to 133% of poverty and refundable premium tax credits up to 400% of poverty. People with preexisting conditions gain guaranteed access to coverage. Young adults can stay on a parent's plan until 26. Seniors get a Medicare drug coverage gap discount and free preventive care. Small businesses get a tax credit covering up to 50% of employee health costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicaid to everyone under 65 with incomes at or below 133% of the federal poverty line, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of newly eligible people from 2014 to 2016.
Gives refundable tax credits for premiums and caps out-of-pocket costs for households earning between 100% and 400% of the poverty line buying coverage through new state Exchanges.

Bans health plans from excluding preexisting conditions, rescinding coverage except for fraud, or setting annual and lifetime dollar limits on essential benefits, and requires free coverage of recommended preventive services.

Lets unmarried adult children stay on a parent's health plan until age 26, and creates a temporary high-risk pool covering uninsured people with preexisting conditions starting within 90 days of enactment.

Requires health plans to spend at least 80-85% of premium dollars on medical care and quality improvement, refunding the difference to enrollees, and requires every US hospital to publish its standard charges.

Raises Medicaid drug rebates and requires brand-name drug makers to discount drugs for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap, and lets cheaper biosimilar versions of expensive biologic drugs be approved for the first time.
Gives small employers with up to 25 employees a tax credit for up to 50% of employee health coverage costs.
Adds transparency rules requiring drug and device makers to disclose payments to physicians, and requires nursing homes to disclose ownership, publish staffing data, and face tougher penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Most people who remain uninsured pay a tax penalty. High earners pay an added 0.9% Medicare tax over $200,000/$250,000 of income. Employers with more than 50 full-time workers who don't offer coverage pay fines. Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and medical device makers pay annual fees; employers with the most generous plans pay a 40% excise tax on the excess. Taxpayers fund the Medicaid expansion and premium credits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Uninsured individuals, high earners, large employers, and health industries

drawbacks.text: Starting in 2014, individuals must carry minimum essential coverage or pay a penalty, though people who cannot afford coverage, tribal members, people in hardship, religious objectors, undocumented immigrants, and the incarcerated are exempt.

Instead of a government-run plan, the law routes subsidies through private insurers and requires plans to certify as qualified health plans to sell them, making private insurers the permanent channel for the new coverage.
The law gives brand-name biologic drug makers 12 years before a cheaper biosimilar copy can be approved, longer protection than advocates for cheaper drugs sought.

Annual fees on health insurers, drug makers, and device makers are widely expected to be reflected in premiums and prices, and the law itself requires a study of whether employer fines are passed to workers through lower wages.

It cuts Medicare payments to hospitals serving many uninsured patients (DSH) as the insured population grows, and bases Medicare Advantage payments on competitive bids, reducing what those private plans receive.
It contains a state-specific provision giving Nebraska 100% federal funding for its Medicaid expansion from 2017, which other states' senators criticized during floor debate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: tens of millions of uninsured people become eligible for subsidized coverage, and insurers can no longer deny or cap care for people who get sick. The costs are also real: a new mandate on individuals, fines on larger employers, industry fees that may show up in premiums, higher Medicare taxes for top earners, and a design choice that funnels public money through private insurance companies rather than a public plan. The 12-year exclusivity for brand biologics is a genuine concession to drug makers that delays cheaper competition.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate used an unrelated House tax bill as a vehicle, passed its health care rewrite 60-39 after Christmas-eve debate, the House accepted the Senate version 219-212 in March 2010, and the President signed it into law.

narrative.text: The bill began as the Service Members Home Ownership Tax Act of 2009, a House tax bill for military homebuyers.
The House passed that original bill 416-0 on October 8, 2009, with 243 Democrats and 173 Republicans voting yes.

The Senate then rewrote the bill into the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. It first cleared a 60-vote threshold just to take up the bill, 60-39 on November 21, with every Republican opposed.
Senate Republicans repeatedly offered motions to send the bill back to committee; five such motions failed on December 3-15, 2009.

Cloture to end debate was invoked 60-39 on December 23, and the Senate passed the amended bill 60-39 in the early hours of December 24, 2009, with all 58 Democrats and both independents for and all 39 Republicans against.
On March 21, 2010, the House agreed to the Senate amendments 219-212: all 219 yes votes were Democrats, while 178 Republicans and 34 Democrats voted no.
President Obama signed the bill on March 23, 2010, making it Public Law 111-148.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Millions of uninsured and low-income people who became eligible for coverage, and people with preexisting conditions who can no longer be denied insurance, are better off. Health insurers also came out ahead, since the mandate and subsidies make private plans the permanent channel for the new coverage, though they face new fees and rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Newly covered patients and health insurers

industries.note: The law makes private insurance plans the permanent channel for newly subsidized coverage: subsidies and the individual mandate route millions of customers to private issuers. In exchange, insurers accept annual fees, minimum medical-spending ratios with rebates, a ban on preexisting-condition denials, and a cap on insurer executive pay deductions.

Drug makers pay an annual fee on branded sales, higher Medicaid rebates, and discounts for seniors in the coverage gap, but gained a 12-year exclusivity period before cheaper biosimilar copies can be approved, delaying price competition.

The law rebases Medicare Advantage payments on competitive bids and cuts the payment formula, reducing federal overpayments to private Medicare plans; the bill bars plans from passing higher cost-sharing for chemotherapy, dialysis, and nursing care onto beneficiaries.
The law imposes an annual fee on manufacturers and importers of medical devices beginning in 2011, as part of paying for the coverage expansion.

Employers with more than 200 full-time workers must auto-enroll employees and those with more than 50 face fines for not offering coverage or long waiting periods; small employers instead get a tax credit for up to 50% of coverage costs.

Hospitals must publish standard charges, face readmission penalties and charitable-care requirements, and take cuts to Medicare and Medicaid payments for uncompensated care, but they gain millions of newly insured paying customers.

Charitable hospitals must run community health needs assessments, adopt financial assistance policies, and refrain from aggressive collections against patients who may qualify for aid, with a penalty tax for noncompliance.
